pages.name: The gear pair
pages.text: The bigger gear turns slower, by the ratio of the teeth. At the small dot where the teeth meet, each tooth on the 20-tooth [[pinion]] pushes one tooth on the 100-tooth [[wheel]] past. So both gears' teeth move at the same speed there. The pinion turns five times to pass all 100 teeth. The [[gear ratio]] is the driven gear's teeth ÷ the driving gear's: 100 ÷ 20 = 5. More teeth on the wheel make the pump shaft turn slower and push harder.
pages.alt: A 20-tooth pinion on the motor drives a 100-tooth wheel on the pump shaft. Curved arrows show each shaft's speed and torque, and a bar below shows the power passing through.

pages.name: Wheel speed
pages.task: A 15-tooth pinion turns at 1450 rev/min. It drives a 45-tooth wheel. How fast does the wheel turn?
pages.why: The ratio is 45 ÷ 15 = 3. The pinion must turn three times to pass all 45 of the wheel's teeth. So the wheel turns at 1450 ÷ 3 = 483 rev/min.
pages.alt: A 15-tooth pinion turning at 1450 revolutions a minute drives a 45-tooth wheel, whose speed is asked.

pages.name: The push at the mesh
pages.text: The torque rises by the same ratio of 5. The reason lies at the mesh. The pinion's teeth sit 0.04 m from its centre. So the motor's 72.4 N m pushes them with 72.4 ÷ 0.04 = 1810 N. That push acts on the wheel's tooth. The wheel's tooth pushes back just as hard. But the wheel's tooth sits 0.2 m from its centre, five times as far out. So the wheel's torque is 1810 × 0.2 = 362 N m. Here nothing is lost to friction.
pages.alt: At the mesh the pinion's tooth pushes the wheel's tooth with 1810 newtons, and is pushed back as hard. The pinion's radius is 0.04 metres and the wheel's 0.2 metres.

pages.name: Wheel torque
pages.task: The same 15 and 45-tooth pair has 20 N m on its pinion. Nothing is lost to friction. What torque does the wheel's shaft carry?
pages.why: The ratio is 45 ÷ 15 = 3. The wheel's teeth sit three times as far from its centre as the pinion's. The same push at the mesh gives three times the torque: 20 × 3 = 60 N m.
pages.alt: A 15-tooth pinion with 20 newton metres on it drives a 45-tooth wheel, whose torque is asked.

pages.name: Power passes through
pages.text: Power is torque × angular speed, with the speed in rad/s. Five times the torque at a fifth of the speed is the same power. So a gearbox cannot make power. Friction turns a little of it into heat. At 100% efficiency the full 11 kW passes through. At an example 95%, 550 W is lost at the mesh. The pump gets 10.45 kW. With 20 and 100 teeth, its torque drops from 362 N m to 344 N m. A lower efficiency turns more of the power into heat.
pages.alt: A 20-tooth pinion on the motor drives a 100-tooth wheel on the pump shaft. Curved arrows show each shaft's speed and torque, and a bar below shows the power passing through.

pages.name: Power out
pages.task: 15 kW goes into a 4 : 1 gearbox. Its efficiency is 96%. How much power reaches the output shaft?
pages.why: A gearbox trades speed for torque, but it cannot make power. The power out is the power in × the efficiency: 15 × 0.96 = 14.4 kW. The rest turns to heat.

pages.name: A second pair
pages.text: Two pairs in a row make a [[compound gear train]]. A second 20-tooth pinion sits on the wheel's shaft. It drives a 60-tooth wheel, a ratio of 3. The pump moves onto that last shaft. The ratios multiply: 5 × 3 = 15. So the pump shaft turns at 1450 ÷ 15 = 96.7 rev/min. Each pair loses its own share of the power. At 95% each, 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.90. So about 90% gets through. The pump shaft carries 981 N m. With one pair only, the ratio is 5.
pages.alt: A 20-tooth pinion on the motor drives a 100-tooth wheel on the pump shaft, then a second pair of 20 and 60 teeth. Curved arrows show each shaft's speed and torque, and a bar below shows the power passing through.

pages.name: Two pairs
pages.task: A motor at 1440 rev/min drives a 4 : 1 pair, then a 6 : 1 pair. How fast does the output shaft turn?
pages.why: The ratios multiply: 4 × 6 = 24. So the output turns at 1440 ÷ 24 = 60 rev/min. Pair by pair, 1440 ÷ 4 = 360, then 360 ÷ 6 = 60.

pages.name: A belt
pages.text: A [[belt]] works the same way. If it does not slip, it moves at the speed of both pulley rims. So a belt's ratio is the driven pulley's diameter ÷ the driving pulley's diameter. Here that is 400 ÷ 80 = 5, the same as the gears. A plain loop of belt, called an open belt, turns both pulleys the same way. Two gears meshing on their outsides turn opposite ways. Gears give the same ratio, but turn the pump shaft the other way.

pages.name: Belt speed
pages.task: A 100 mm motor pulley turns at 1450 rev/min. A belt drives a 250 mm fan pulley. How fast does the fan turn?
pages.why: The belt moves at the speed of both pulley rims. The ratio is 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5. So the fan turns at 1450 ÷ 2.5 = 580 rev/min.

pages.name: Lining up shafts
pages.text: A [[coupling]] joins the ends of two shafts so one drives the other. The two shafts' centre lines must lie in one straight line, within a small tolerance. Shafts that meet at an angle, or sit parallel but offset, have [[misalignment]]. It barely changes the motor's efficiency. The harm is wear and heat. It brings vibration, noise and hot bearings. It wears out bearings, couplings and shafts early.

pages.name: Winch drum
pages.task: A 4 kW motor at 960 rev/min drives a winch drum through a 4 : 1 gearbox. Nothing is lost to friction. What torque does the drum shaft carry?
pages.why: The drum turns at 960 ÷ 4 = 240 rev/min. That is 240 × 2π ÷ 60 = 25.13 rad/s. Torque is power ÷ angular speed. So the drum carries 4000 ÷ 25.13 = 159 N m.

pages.name: A hot coupling
pages.task: A pump's coupling and bearings run hot after a refit. A check finds the two shafts parallel, but one sits 0.5 mm higher. What is wrong?
pages.why: The centre lines must lie in one straight line. Here they are parallel but 0.5 mm apart. That is parallel misalignment. It brings vibration, noise and heat, and wears out bearings and couplings early.
